prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Please, Read, Wraith

outputs.L1:
Please, God, love me and buy me.  
Read this hillock and ride me, Wraith,  
typing all day for money.

God bought me today  
for two silver fish in a can.  
God bought me tomorrow  
for bland in a pan  
and a card—  
an email from Rebecca.

Bought four hours of my control-alt-delete shutdown.  
Bought a new day-section with a headstand.  
My commerce in shall sky like a grandstand.  
Transact.

God performed me today  
for a half-minute lucky in a locker room,  
hiding my boobs from the kids,  
and my hair is silky,  
and my mane shot-silk gold.

Bought a book on economy:  
Georgie Bataille.  
Called about plane tickets:  
Georgie Bataille.  
I bought my debt today:  
Georgie Bataille, hooray.

Debt off my God today.  
God off my debt in a macular hole.

I dream of an end like a fount to this night:  
run thinner and thinner,  
and then it’s all light.

Macerated in signal by my go.  
I bought my ghost.  
I walk my ghost.
outputs.L2:
God, please care for me and purchase me.  
Read this little mound and carry me along.  
A Wraith spends the whole day typing for cash.  

Today, God paid for me with two canned silver fish.  
Tomorrow, God will pay for me with something tasteless in a pan,  
plus a card,  
plus an email from Rebecca.  

Four hours of my control-alt-delete shutdown were bought.  
A fresh portion of the day was purchased, complete with a headstand.  
My trade will rise into the sky like stadium seating.  

Transaction.  
God enacted me today for half a fortunate minute  
in a locker room, concealing my breasts from the children,  
while my hair was smooth,  
my mane bright as gold shot through silk.  

I purchased an economics book by Georges Bataille.  
I made a call about airplane tickets.  
Georges Bataille.  

Today I bought my debt.  
Georges Bataille, hooray.  
My debt is lifted from God today.  
God is removed from my debt inside a macular hole.  

I imagine an ending to this night like water springing from a source:  
it grows finer and finer  
until everything becomes light.  

Soaked and broken down in signal by my own going,  
I bought my ghost.  
I walk with my ghost.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents love, faith, and commerce as deeply intertwined forces, each capable of claiming ownership over the speaker’s life. Rather than treating emotion, belief, and money as separate realms, the speaker suggests that they operate together, shaping identity through exchange, obligation, and control. Love is not only an intimate feeling, faith is not only a spiritual commitment, and commerce is not only an economic system; all three become ways in which the self is purchased, divided, or surrendered.

Throughout the poem, images of work, debt, and transaction are repeatedly linked to spiritual and personal submission. The speaker seems caught in a world where every action has a cost and every relationship involves some form of payment. Labor becomes more than physical or economic activity: it becomes a metaphor for devotion, sacrifice, and exhaustion. Debt, similarly, is not merely financial but emotional and spiritual, suggesting that the speaker owes parts of themselves to others, to systems, or to belief itself. This creates a sense that the self is never fully free, but always bound by invisible contracts.

The references to Georges Bataille and economy deepen this meditation on value, sacrifice, and excess. Bataille’s ideas often challenge ordinary notions of usefulness and profit, focusing instead on waste, expenditure, eroticism, and sacred loss. By invoking this framework, the poem suggests that human life cannot be understood only through practical or capitalist measures of value. Love and faith may involve forms of giving that exceed reason, just as sacrifice involves the loss of something precious. The poem therefore questions what it means to be valuable, what must be given up, and whether surrender can ever be separated from desire.

At the same time, the speaker’s experience is intensely bodily. Images of hiding, hair, and physical exposure convey vulnerability and self-consciousness. The body appears as something both intimate and visible, something the speaker inhabits but also feels watched through. Hair may suggest privacy, sensuality, shame, or concealment, while exposure points to the fear of being seen too clearly. These bodily images ground the poem’s abstract concerns in lived experience, showing how economic, spiritual, and emotional pressures are felt on and through the body.

By the end, the poem moves toward a desire for release and transformation. The speaker seems to long for escape from the systems of debt, labor, visibility, and possession that have shaped their life. This release is imagined not simply as freedom in a social sense, but as dissolution: a wish to become light, ghostly, or less materially bound. The ending suggests a yearning to move beyond the body, beyond ownership, and beyond the demands of value. In this final movement, the poem transforms surrender into something more ambiguous: not only defeat, but also the possibility of becoming weightless, radiant, and unclaimed.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a fragmented and unsettling meditation on the speaker’s relationship with God, labor, debt, and selfhood. Rather than describing faith, work, or identity in stable, familiar terms, it filters them through the language of transaction: buying, selling, owing, performing, and being consumed. The speaker appears trapped in a world where everything has become commodified, including the soul, the body, and even the possibility of spiritual connection. God is not approached simply as a source of comfort or salvation, but as part of an economy of exchange, obligation, and negotiation. Prayer and devotion begin to resemble bargaining, while existence itself feels like a debt that must be paid.

This transactional logic shapes the speaker’s understanding of labor. Work is not presented as meaningful or dignified, but as repetitive, draining, and tied to systems of control. The speaker’s actions suggest a cycle of performance: they must continually offer themselves, sell parts of themselves, or become useful in order to survive. Labor becomes inseparable from identity, as if the speaker can only know who they are through what they produce, what they owe, or what others can extract from them. The body and self are treated almost like objects on a market, broken into pieces and assigned value.

The text’s surreal and fragmented imagery reflects this damaged condition. Its disjointed structure mirrors a consciousness under pressure, one that cannot fully separate spiritual desire from economic necessity. Images of commerce, divinity, exhaustion, and bodily transformation collide with one another, creating a world where the sacred and the material have become disturbingly fused. The speaker’s longing for God may still be genuine, but it is distorted by the conditions surrounding it. Faith is no longer pure refuge; it has been absorbed into the same systems of debt and exchange that govern the rest of life.

As a result, the speaker’s sense of self becomes unstable. If everything can be bought or sold, then identity itself begins to feel uncertain. The repeated acts of transaction imply that the speaker is both participant and victim: they sell, perform, and bargain, but they are also being sold, used, and emptied out. This creates a powerful feeling of alienation. The speaker is estranged from God, from labor, from the body, and from their own inner life. They seem to exist in a state of partial disappearance, no longer fully present as a whole person.

The final image of the “ghost” brings these tensions together. On one level, the ghost represents the speaker’s alienation: they have been made spectral by economic and spiritual exhaustion, reduced to a trace of themselves after repeated acts of exchange. The ghost suggests that the speaker has been hollowed out by debt, labor, and performance. Yet the image also carries a possible desire for release. To become a ghost may mean escaping the body, escaping obligation, or slipping beyond the systems that have assigned value to every part of existence. The ghost is therefore both a sign of loss and a fragile form of freedom.

Overall, the text suggests that spiritual longing and personal identity cannot remain untouched in a world governed by economic exchange. The speaker’s relationship with God is shaped by the same forces that shape labor and debt, turning even transcendence into a kind of transaction. Through its fragmented, surreal, and transactional imagery, the text portrays a self struggling to survive under conditions that reduce everything to value. The speaker’s final ghostly state reveals the cost of that reduction: the person remains present, but only as an absence, a remnant, or a longing for escape.
outputs.L5:
**Please Read: The Wraith**

Please, read this warning carefully.

They say the wraith appears only when the moon is hidden and the wind moves without sound. It does not walk through the forest—it drifts, pale and silent, between the trees like a forgotten memory. Those who have seen it describe a figure wrapped in shadow, with eyes that glow like dying stars.

No one knows where the wraith came from. Some believe it was once a lost traveler, trapped between the world of the living and the dead. Others say it is a guardian, protecting an ancient secret buried beneath the hills. But everyone agrees on one thing: if you hear your name whispered in the dark, do not answer.

Please, if you ever find an old sign that says “Read before entering,” do not ignore it. The warning may be the only thing standing between you and the wraith.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in a frantic, stream-of-consciousness voice mixing religion, commerce, debt, office work, and bodily vulnerability, with repeated phrases about God buying the speaker and references to Georges Bataille.
counterfactuals.output:
God bought me at the quarterly review, God bought me with the petty cash, God bought me and filed the receipt under MISCELLANEOUS MERCY, and now I am stapled to the morning, now I am three-hole-punched and singing through the holes, O Lord of invoices, O fluorescent dove, O manager of my trembling flesh—

I woke up owing everyone my skin.

The body is a cubicle with a leaking ceiling. The soul is a spreadsheet with hidden columns. My mouth is an envelope licked shut by someone else. Georges Bataille is in the break room eating lightbulbs and speaking of expenditure, sacred waste, the ecstatic bankruptcy of the self; he says the sun spends without accounting, the sun does not clock in, the sun has no supervisor, and I nod, I nod, I nod while copying my own confession to Accounts Payable.

God bought me. God bought me. God bought me at a discount.

There was a sale on the second floor: absolution, toner cartridges, ergonomic chairs, lambs without blemish, lambs with purchase orders, lambs crying softly into the shared printer. The receptionist wore seven crowns and a headset. She said, Your call is important to us. She said, Please hold for judgment. She said, All debts are spiritual debts, and all spiritual debts accrue interest after thirty days.

I tried to hide my hands beneath the desk but my hands were already in litigation, my knees were collateral, my throat had been refinanced. Every organ signed in blue ink. My ribs were thin as paper clips. My heart kept sending calendar invites titled APOCALYPSE / MANDATORY / NO LUNCH PROVIDED.

God bought me with blood or credit or some radiant procurement card. God bought me and I cannot find the return policy.

Bataille laughs from the supply closet, naked except for a badge that says VISITOR. He opens a box of communion wafers marked FRAGILE and scatters them like coins. He says the sacred is not clean, the sacred is a wound in the budget, the sacred is the boss lifting his face from the annual report to reveal the face of a goat, the face of a child, the face of a coin spinning forever between heads and tails.

I am late, I am late, I am late for the crucifixion meeting.

My inbox fills with psalms and overdraft notices. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the remaining balance. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall be contacted by collections. Blessed is the employee who remembers to attach the attachment. Blessed is the bleeding animal who still submits the form by Friday.

God bought me, yes, yes, God bought me, but who appraised this shaking merchandise? Who priced the fever? Who counted my teeth? Who inventoried the little panic living under my tongue?

At noon the office becomes a cathedral becomes a marketplace becomes a stomach. The copier hums like a hive of penitents. The vending machine dispenses indulgences in foil packets. Someone from Legal washes his hands and the water comes out wine, then ink, then rainwater from the century I was born in. I kneel beside the wastebasket full of shredded contracts and pray to be illegible.

Because I am tired of being legible.

Because every ledger wants a body.

Because even heaven has a payroll department and even angels need direct deposit and even martyrs must submit receipts for mileage.

God bought me. God bought me. God bought me and placed me on hold inside my own bones.

O Bataille of the excess, Bataille of the impossible, Bataille with his eye pressed to the keyhole of the sacred, tell me how to spend myself until no creditor can name me. Tell me how to squander the fear. Tell me how the wound becomes a door and the door becomes a mouth and the mouth says not profit, not productivity, not performance metrics, but flame, but laughter, but the useless gorgeous pouring-out of being.

The CEO descends in a cloud of quarterly earnings. His tie is a serpent. His smile is a covenant. He says we are a family here, which is why the knives are communal. He says there will be restructuring. He says sacrifice is necessary. He says please initial beside each plague.

My shirt sticks to my back. My body betrays me with sweat, pulse, hunger, softness. I am not a concept, I whisper to the stapler. I am not an asset class. I am not a line item in the Book of Life. I am a breakable mammal under bad lighting, full of salt and unpaid prayers.

Still: God bought me.

Still: the debt sings.

Still: Bataille is dancing on the conference table, scattering coins into the mouths of the dead, shouting that nothing holy can be saved, only spent, spent, spent—

And I, purchased and perishable, stamped APPROVED in red across the chest, run laughing through the cubicles with my invoice burning behind me, my wounds wide open to the market, to the altar, to the terrible sun that gives and gives and never asks to be reimbursed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a chaotic avant-garde monologue from the perspective of someone feeling purchased by God, trapped in work and transactions, blending mystical language with mundane details like email, plane tickets, canned fish, and locker rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
I was bought at dawn, I think—  
not redeemed, not rescued, not wrapped in linen,  
but purchased, scanned, approved,  
a little green checkmark blooming in the terminal of heaven.

God stood there with a receipt in His teeth.  
God had my invoice number.  
God said: **nonrefundable.**  
God said: **you agreed to the terms by continuing to breathe.**

And now I go to work.

I go to work with my soul in a plastic badge holder,  
clipped to my belt loop, swinging against my thigh like a minor bell.  
I answer email from inside the whale.  
Subject line: *Following up.*  
Subject line: *Quick question.*  
Subject line: *Can we circle back?*  
The seraphim have Outlook calendars.  
The cherubim use color-coded tags.  
My manager says we are all replaceable  
and I hear the great wheels of Ezekiel squeak in the ceiling vent.

There is no outside anymore.  
There is only the transaction:  
tap card, submit form, initial here,  
accept cookies, accept suffering, accept the mystery,  
accept that your body is a leased instrument  
with a deductible and a lunch break.

At 2:13 p.m. I eat canned fish over the sink  
because the break room smells like warm plastic and old promises.  
Sardines in olive oil, bright as little martyrs.  
Their eyes say: we too were gathered.  
We too were sealed in metal.  
We too believed the sea was permanent.

I have a plane ticket in my inbox  
and nowhere to go.

Departure: imminent.  
Gate: unannounced.  
Seat: middle, between commerce and revelation.  
Boarding group: the exhausted.  
Carry-on: one trembling animal called a heart,  
one quart-sized bag of sanctioned liquids,  
one folded shirt still damp from the locker room  
where men stand under fluorescent judgment  
and talk about interest rates, fantasy football, back pain,  
the mysterious rash of the mortal enterprise.

In the locker room, the tiles are wet with baptism and athlete’s foot.  
Steam rises like confused incense.  
A man snaps a towel and says, “You working late?”  
and I want to answer:  
Brother, I have been working since Genesis.  
I have been clocked in since the first light punched through the dark.  
My timesheet is a scroll unrolling into fire.

But I say, “Probably.”

Because this is how the purchased speak.  
Softly. Efficiently. With bullet points.

God owns the silence between my keystrokes.  
God owns the stale coffee in the conference room.  
God owns the password I forgot and the password I became.  
God owns the ergonomic chair, the toner dust,  
the sad banana bruising in my bag,  
the automatic door that opens only when I pretend not to need it.

Everywhere: price tags on invisible things.

A smile costs compliance.  
A paycheck costs posture.  
A prayer costs language.  
A body costs maintenance.  
A soul costs everything and still arrives late,  
still gets marked incomplete,  
still receives the email: *Please revise and resubmit.*

I have tried to void the sale.

I have stood at customer service beneath the humming lights  
holding my own face in both hands.  
I have said: There has been a mistake.  
I have said: I did not order this loneliness.  
I have said: The product arrived damaged.  
I have said: The instructions were in thunder.  
I have said: The warranty mentions resurrection  
but only in metaphor.

The clerk was an angel with acrylic nails.  
She looked me up in the system.  
She frowned.  
She said, “It says here you belong to Him.”

To Him.

Capital H like a hook in the sky.

So I return to the cubicle cathedral.  
I genuflect before the login screen.  
I attach the attachment I forgot to attach.  
I become carbon-copied, archived, searchable.  
My hands move over the keyboard like insects over scripture.  
Somewhere a printer jams with the passion of a prophet.  
Somewhere a microwave counts down from 30  
with the patience of an executioner.

And still, sometimes, in the vending machine glass,  
between the protein bars and the salted peanuts,  
I see a burning bush.

Not burning, exactly.  
More like flickering.  
More like the cheap light failing.  
More like a message trying to get through the wire:

You are not the work.  
You are not the purchase order.  
You are not the ticket, the aisle, the boarding pass,  
the meeting invite, the canned fish,  
the locker combination, the wet towel on the floor.

But then the machine takes my dollar  
and gives me nothing.

And I laugh.

I laugh so hard the elevators stop between floors.  
I laugh until the saints in the smoke detector blink red.  
I laugh because God has bought me  
and I am still somehow always paying.  
I laugh because my freedom has a tracking number.  
I laugh because the kingdom is coming  
and I have a 9 a.m. with procurement.

O Lord of receipts,  
O Buyer beyond buying,  
O terrible Accountant of sparrows,  
if I am Yours, then explain this barcode on my wrist.  
Explain this hunger with a calendar invite.  
Explain why the sacred arrives dressed as obligation,  
why grace smells faintly of disinfectant,  
why my name in Your mouth sounds like a confirmation code.

The plane ticket remains unused.  
The sardine tin shines in the trash like a small dead moon.  
The email refreshes.  
The locker door slams.  
The world says: next customer.

And I step forward.  
I step forward because I was called.  
I step forward because I was bought.  
I step forward because the line behind me is infinite  
and everyone is holding something tender  
they cannot afford to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nonsensical but emotionally intense text fragment about divine love, money, debt, and identity dissolution, with Bataille references and phrases that feel like corrupted dictation or dream logic.
counterfactuals.output:
God kept calling me by my invoice number, and I answered because the name my mother gave me had already been garnished.

Love came down like a gold tooth in the rain, like a wet receipt from heaven, like Bataille laughing into the wound where the bank used to be. I said: Lord, if you are love, why do you accrue interest? And the Lord said something ruined by static, something like **expenditure is the only prayer / the sun is a debt that never asks to be repaid / your face has been repossessed**.

I was kneeling in the red office of the heart. The clerks had no eyes. They stamped my childhood **PAID IN SACRIFICE** and then stamped it again **INSUFFICIENT FUNDS**. Every stamp sounded like a kiss. Every kiss became a little bankruptcy of the self.

Bataille said the sacred is excess, or maybe my phone said it, overheating in the bathtub, whispering: squander yourself, become unusable, become feast. Divine love does not save; it spends. It pours out the “I” like coins from a torn pocket, bright useless moons rolling under the furniture of the cosmos.

I loved God so much I became counterfeit. I loved money so much it became flesh. I loved my debt so much it called me father. Then all my identities softened, their labels running in the rain: debtor, beloved, animal, creditor, wound, bride, meat with a signature.

“Please state your full legal soul,” said the angel at collections.

But my mouth was full of luminous pennies. My tongue had dissolved into a small nation of beggars. I tried to say **I am**, but it came out **I owe, I owe, I owe**, and the choir repeated it until the ceiling opened and the sky leaned down, tender and obscene, to forgive me incorrectly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
